messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Margaret is a 69-year-old agricultural worker who has spent decades harvesting crops in rural California. The trauma happened five years ago, when a younger coworker she had trusted cornered her in a storage shed after a long day. He assaulted her while she pleaded for him to stop, and afterward she told no one, certain she would be blamed. She left that farm and found work at another, hoping the memory would fade, but it did not. The memory surfaced without warning—while she rode the bus to work, the sight of a man in a similar cap brought the shed back vividly. Buses became a trigger, as did any conversation about workplace safety or male kindness, which made the shame feel fresh. When these triggers hit, Margaret’s immediate response was to reach for alcohol. She would pour a glass of wine as soon as she got home, or she would sit and mentally rehearse the worst possible outcomes of her day—preparing herself for another attack so she wouldn’t be caught off guard. She also began avoiding people entirely, canceling plans with friends and skipping church. The triggers also stirred up intense threat reactions. After a memory intruded, she would find herself looking behind her constantly, checking if someone was following, even in the grocery store. Her heart would race, and she felt a mix of fear and guilt—fear of another attack, guilt that she hadn’t fought back. She came to believe she could not rely on herself; after all, she had frozen during the assault, and now she couldn’t control her own mind. Margaret felt like a permanent outsider, set apart from others who had not experienced such violation. This sense of isolation made her especially sensitive to any conversational topic that touched on vulnerability, which would then trigger another intrusive memory, cementing the cycle. Her negative appraisals drove her maladaptive strategies directly. Because she believed she could not rely on herself, she rehearsed worst-case scenarios obsessively, trying to be ready. And because she saw herself as an outsider, avoidance felt natural—why expose herself to more judgment? But the strategies backfired. The mental rehearsal often brought the original assault to mind in vivid detail, acting as its own trigger. Drinking dulled her vigilance but then left her feeling vulnerable, which increased her perception of threat. Carrying that constant sense of threat, she found that even harmless sights—a figure in the distance, a door left ajar—now registered as warnings. Avoidance meant that when she did have to go out—to work, to the pharmacy—her anxiety was sky-high, and she would scan her surroundings constantly. Scanning for danger itself became a trigger: catching a glimpse of a man who looked like her attacker would flood the memory back. Now Margaret’s world has shrunk. She only feels safe in her own home and her daughter’s house. Her husband drives her to work because she can no longer tolerate the bus. She has stopped attending family gatherings, afraid a conversation will bring the shame to the surface. Last week, a neighbor made a casual comment about “looking over your shoulder,” and Margaret broke down sobbing. That night she drank more than usual and could not sleep. Her husband urged her to see a doctor, and she agreed, though she is terrified that talking about the assault will only make the memories worse. She hopes, somewhere, that there might be a way to feel less like an outsider, but she is not sure she can trust herself to get better.
